(a) None of the funds appropriated in this or any other Act may be used to take any action to modify—
        (1) the appropriations account structure for the National Intelligence Program budget, including through the creation of a new appropriation or new appropriation account; 
        (2) how the National Intelligence Program budget request is presented in the unclassified P–1, R–1, and O–1 documents supporting the Department of Defense budget request; 
        (3) the process by which the National Intelligence Program appropriations are apportioned to the executing agencies; or 
        (4) the process by which the National Intelligence Program appropriations are allotted, obligated and disbursed.  
    (b) Nothing in subsection (a) shall be construed to prohibit the merger of programs or changes to the National Intelligence Program budget at or below the Expenditure Center level, provided 
such change is otherwise in accordance with paragraphs (a)(1)–(3). 
    (c) The Director of National Intelligence and the Secretary of Defense may jointly, only for the purposes of achieving auditable financial statements and improving fiscal reporting, study and develop detailed proposals for alternative financial management processes. Such study shall include a comprehensive counterintelligence risk assessment to ensure that none of the alternative processes will adversely affect counterintelligence. 
    (d) Upon development of the detailed proposals defined under subsection (c), the Director of National Intelligence and the Secretary of Defense shall—
        (1) provide the proposed alternatives to all affected agencies; 
        (2) receive certification from all affected agencies attesting that the proposed alternatives will help achieve auditability, improve fiscal reporting, and will not adversely affect counterintelligence; and 
        (3) not later than 30 days after receiving all necessary certifications under paragraph (2), present the proposed alternatives and certifications to the congressional defense and intelligence committees.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that sharing proposals with "affected agencies", receiving their certifications, and presenting them to congressional committees is consultation. Every actor involved (the Director of National Intelligence, the Secretary of Defense, the affected executing agencies, and the congressional committees) is inside the federal government. No state, tribe, company, expert, or member of the public is brought into any decision, and no rulemaking, hearing, or right to sue is created.
fable.s: present the proposed alternatives and certifications to the congressional defense and intelligence committees

opus.w: The only process here is the Director of National Intelligence and the Secretary of Defense sharing proposals with affected federal agencies, getting certifications from them, and presenting the results to congressional committees. All of these actors are inside the federal government. The procedural words ('certification,' 'present... to the congressional... committees') might suggest participation, but coordination within the government and reports to Congress fall under the listed exclusions, and no outside party is involved.
opus.b: The tempting reading is "Yes": the section has a study, proposals sent to "all affected agencies," certifications from those agencies, and a presentation to congressional committees, which looks like a formal consultation process. That reading fails because everyone involved is inside the federal government. The Director of National Intelligence, the Secretary of Defense, the affected executive agencies and the congressional defense and intelligence committees are all federal. Nothing brings in states, experts, companies or the public, and there is no rulemaking, hearing, comment period or right to sue.

qwen_chat.w: The section requires coordination between federal officials (Director of National Intelligence, Secretary of Defense) and other federal agencies ('affected agencies'), as well as reporting to Congress. All these actors are inside the federal government. There is no requirement to consult with states, tribes, the public, or other non-federal entities before making a decision.
qwen_chat.s: (d) Upon development of the detailed proposals defined under subsection (c), the Director of National Intelligence and the Secretary of Defense shall— (1) provide the proposed alternatives to all affected agencies; (2) receive certification from all affected agencies attesting that the proposed alternatives will help achieve auditability, improve fiscal reporting, and will not adversely affect counterintelligence; and (3) not later than 30 days after receiving all necessary certifications under paragraph (2), present the proposed alternatives and certifications to the congressional defense and intelligence committees.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that subsection (d)(1) and (d)(2) require the Director of National Intelligence and the Secretary of Defense to provide proposals to "all affected agencies" and receive certifications from them, which could be seen as coordination with outside entities. However, "affected agencies" in the context of the National Intelligence Program and Department of Defense budget are federal agencies (e.g., CIA, NSA, DIA, etc.). Since these are all inside the federal government, this is intra-governmental coordination, not participation with outside parties. The final step is presenting to Congress, which is also inside the federal government.
